source: NCERT Class 8 Science (Curiosity — Textbook of Science for Grade 8)

questions.question: Anything that has mass and occupies space is called:
questions.explanation: Matter is defined as anything that has mass and occupies space, such as stones, water, and air.

questions.question: What are the tiny basic building blocks that make up any piece of matter called?
questions.explanation: A constituent particle is the basic unit that makes up a larger piece of any substance or material.

questions.question: In Activity 7.1, grinding a stick of chalk into fine powder using a mortar and pestle is which type of change?
questions.explanation: Grinding chalk only reduces the size of its pieces without forming any new substance, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Can we see the constituent particles of chalk or sugar through an ordinary microscope?
options: Yes, easily with a hand lens
Yes, with an ordinary school microscope
No, they are too small even for an ordinary microscope
questions.explanation: Constituent particles of matter are extremely small and cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope.

questions.question: Which ancient Indian philosopher first proposed the idea of 'Parmanu'?
questions.explanation: Acharya Kanad first spoke about the idea of Parmanu (atom) as tiny, indivisible, eternal particles of matter.

questions.question: In which ancient Indian text did Acharya Kanad write about 'Parmanu'?
questions.explanation: Acharya Kanad wrote about the concept of Parmanu in his treatise called the Vaisheshika Sutras.

questions.question: According to Acharya Kanad, 'Parmanu' are:
questions.explanation: Acharya Kanad described Parmanu as tiny, indivisible, and eternal particles that make up all matter.

questions.question: In Activity 7.2, after sugar dissolves completely in water and disappears, how do we know it is still present at the top?
options: Tasting a spoonful from the top tastes sweet
questions.explanation: Even though dissolved sugar is invisible, tasting the top layer proves its particles have spread throughout the water.

questions.question: Before stirring sugar placed at the bottom of a glass of water, why does the top layer NOT taste sweet?
options: Sugar particles have not yet spread up to the top layer
questions.explanation: Before stirring, the sugar sits at the bottom and its particles have not yet separated and spread to the top layer.

questions.question: How many constituent particles make up a single tiny grain of sugar?
questions.explanation: Each tiny visible grain of sugar is made up of millions and millions of extremely small constituent particles.

questions.question: Is a single fine grain of sand or clay the smallest unit of a rock?
options: Only clay has particles, not sand
Yes, sand cannot be divided further
No, each grain is still made up of a huge number of constituent particles
questions.explanation: Just like chalk powder, fine grains of sand and clay are each made of a huge number of even smaller constituent particles.

questions.question: Which natural process breaks big mountain rocks down into pebbles, stones, sand, and clay?
questions.explanation: In the mountains, rocks break down due to erosion, and flowing rivers grind them further into pebbles, stones, sand, and clay.

questions.question: If we could somehow remove ALL the constituent particles from a wooden chair, what would remain?
options: Only the legs of the chair would remain
The chair would just become lighter
Nothing of the chair would remain
The chair would turn into a liquid
questions.explanation: Because the entire chair is made up of its constituent particles, removing all of them leaves nothing behind.

questions.question: Why does an inflated balloon weigh more than an empty balloon?
options: Light gets trapped inside the balloon
Balloons absorb water from the room
Air is matter made of tiny particles that have mass
questions.explanation: Even though air is invisible, it is matter made of tiny particles that have mass and occupy space.

questions.question: What are the forces that hold the constituent particles of matter together called?
questions.explanation: Constituent particles of matter are held together by attractive forces called interparticle attractions.

questions.question: The strength of interparticle attractions depends on which two factors?
options: Size of the jar and stirring speed
Colour of the substance and shape of the vessel
Weight of the vessel and room light
Nature of the substance and distance between particles
questions.explanation: Interparticle attraction strength depends on the nature of the substance and the interparticle distance.

questions.question: What happens to interparticle forces of attraction if the distance between particles increases even slightly?
questions.explanation: Even a slight increase in interparticle distance decreases the interparticle forces of attraction drastically.

questions.question: Why does ocean water taste salty even though we cannot see any salt crystals in it?
options: Dissolved salt breaks into tiny invisible particles spread throughout the water
Salt turns into a gas in the ocean
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves into tiny invisible constituent particles that occupy the spaces between water particles.

questions.question: What mainly decides whether a substance exists as a solid, liquid, or gas?
options: Whether it is kept in the dark
The strength of interparticle forces of attraction
questions.explanation: The strength of interparticle attractions (which depends on particle spacing and thermal energy) decides the state of matter.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about all three states of matter (solids, liquids, and gases)?
options: Only solids are made of particles
All matter is made up of extremely small particles with spaces between them
Matter has no empty space inside it
Particles exist only when matter is heated
questions.explanation: Solids, liquids, and gases are all made of extremely small constituent particles separated by interparticle spaces.

questions.question: What does the word 'constituent' mean in 'constituent particles of matter'?
options: A basic part that makes up a whole substance
A particle visible to the naked eye
A substance that only exists in water
questions.explanation: Constituent particles (atoms and molecules) are the basic building blocks that make up any material.

questions.question: Which two activities in Chapter 7 first prove that matter is made of extremely small particles?
questions.explanation: Activities 7.1 (breaking/grinding chalk) and 7.2 (dissolving sugar in water) show that matter is composed of extremely small particles.

questions.question: What are the shape and volume of a solid?
options: Neither definite shape nor definite volume
questions.explanation: Solids have both a definite shape and a definite volume because their particles are held tightly in fixed positions.

questions.question: Why do solids like an iron nail, stone, or wooden block keep a fixed shape?
options: Their particles move freely in all directions
They have no particles inside them
Their particles are tightly packed with very strong interparticle attractions
questions.explanation: Very strong interparticle attractions hold solid particles tightly in fixed positions.

questions.question: How do particles move in a solid?
options: They only vibrate (move to and fro) about their fixed positions
They fly freely across the room
They slide smoothly past each other
They jump from one corner to another
questions.explanation: Solid particles cannot move past each other; they only vibrate or oscillate to and fro about their fixed positions.

questions.question: What happens to the particles of a solid when it is heated?
options: They vibrate more vigorously and start leaving their fixed positions
questions.explanation: Heating makes solid particles vibrate vigorously until interparticle attractions weaken and the solid melts.

questions.question: What is the 'melting point' of a solid?
options: Room temperature on a summer day
The temperature at which a gas cools down
The temperature at which a liquid boils
The minimum temperature at which a solid melts into a liquid at atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Melting point is the minimum temperature at which a solid converts into a liquid at atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: According to Table 7.1 of NCERT Class 8 Curiosity, what is the melting point of Ice?
questions.explanation: Table 7.1 lists the melting point of ice as 0 °C.

questions.question: According to Table 7.1 of NCERT Class 8 Curiosity, what is the melting point of Urea?
questions.explanation: Table 7.1 lists the melting points of Ice (0 °C), Urea (133 °C), and Iron (1538 °C).

questions.question: According to Table 7.1 of NCERT Class 8 Curiosity, what is the melting point of Iron?
questions.explanation: Iron has very strong interparticle attractions, giving it a very high melting point of 1538 °C.

questions.question: Usually, particles in a liquid are farther apart than in a solid. Which common substance is an EXCEPTION to this rule?
questions.explanation: Ice is an exception—its particles are farther apart in solid ice than in liquid water.

questions.question: Why does Iron (1538 °C) have a much higher melting point than Ice (0 °C) and Urea (133 °C)?
options: Iron has much stronger interparticle forces of attraction
questions.explanation: Solids with stronger interparticle attractions have higher melting points because more heat is needed to weaken those forces.

questions.question: Arrange Ice, Urea, and Iron in INCREASING order of their interparticle forces of attraction:
questions.explanation: Higher melting point means stronger attraction: Ice (0 °C) < Urea (133 °C) < Iron (1538 °C).

questions.question: What happens to interparticle forces of attraction when a solid melts into a liquid?
questions.explanation: At the melting point, heat energy weakens the interparticle attractions so particles can leave their fixed positions.

questions.question: Rice grains or rice flour take the shape of the jar they are poured into. Are they solids or liquids?
options: Solids, because each individual grain keeps its own fixed shape and volume
Gases, because air sits between grains
Liquids, because they take the jar's shape
questions.explanation: Each individual grain of rice or flour is a solid with a fixed shape and volume; only a heap of many tiny grains takes the jar's shape.

questions.question: Why can you make a heap of stones or sand, but NOT a heap of water?
options: Stones and sand are solids with fixed shapes, while water is a liquid that flows
questions.explanation: Solids keep their fixed shapes and stay piled up, whereas liquid particles slide past each other and flow away.

questions.question: In Activity 7.3, we hammer an iron nail, rock salt, stone, wood, key, and aluminium. What does this show?
options: All solids break into powder equally easily
All solids have strong interparticle forces, though the strength varies by material
Rock salt is harder than iron
questions.explanation: All six are solids with strong interparticle forces, yet materials like iron resist breaking much more strongly than rock salt.

questions.question: Compared to liquids and gases, the interparticle spacing in solids is:
questions.explanation: Among the three states of matter, solids have the minimum interparticle spacing.

questions.question: Compared to liquids and gases, the interparticle forces of attraction in solids are:
questions.explanation: Solids have the strongest interparticle forces of attraction among all three states of matter.

questions.question: Why can you NOT move your finger through a solid wooden block the way you can through water?
options: Strong interparticle attractions hold wood particles firmly in fixed positions
Wood has a low melting point
questions.explanation: In solids, very strong interparticle attractions prevent particles from moving aside when pushed by a finger.

questions.question: Which of the following from Exercise Q7 is a SOLID at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Aluminium foil is a solid with closely packed particles in fixed positions; glycerin is a liquid and methane is a gas.

questions.question: Why do two solid blocks kept side by side NOT mix into each other on their own?
options: Solids repel each other like magnets
Solid particles move faster than gas particles
Solid particles are held tightly in fixed positions and cannot move freely past each other
questions.explanation: Because solid particles only vibrate in fixed positions, they cannot move freely to mix with another solid.

questions.question: In the solid state, the thermal (heat) energy of particles is:
options: Low, allowing only small vibrations in fixed positions
questions.explanation: Low thermal energy keeps solid particles close together under strong attractions, allowing only small vibrations.

questions.question: At a solid's melting point, what is the supplied heat energy used for?
options: To overcome interparticle attractions so the solid becomes a liquid
To turn the solid into iron
questions.explanation: At the melting point, heat energy overcomes the strong interparticle attractions so particles can leave their fixed positions.

questions.question: What are the shape and volume of a liquid?
options: Neither fixed shape nor fixed volume
No fixed shape, but a definite (fixed) volume
questions.explanation: Liquids take the shape of their container (no fixed shape) but always keep the same volume.

questions.question: In Activity 7.4, pouring 200 mL of water into three differently shaped containers (A, B, and C) shows that:
options: Water keeps the same shape in every container
Water changes its volume in each container
Liquids have no fixed shape but have a definite volume
questions.explanation: The water changes shape to match Containers A, B, and C, while its volume remains 200 mL in all three.

questions.question: In Activity 7.4, why might the water level look slightly less than 200 mL after pouring if a container is not clean?
options: Some water sticks to the walls of the previous container
questions.explanation: NCERT notes that if a container is not clean, some water may stick to its walls during pouring.

questions.question: How do particles move in the liquid state?
options: They do not move at all
They are locked in fixed positions
They move freely past each other, but within a limited space
They fly out to fill the whole room instantly
questions.explanation: Liquid particles slide past one another freely, while interparticle attractions keep them within a limited volume.

questions.question: When you move your finger through water in a shallow vessel (Fig. 7.6) and lift it out, what happens?
options: The water freezes around the finger
Water moves aside temporarily and immediately joins back
A permanent cut stays in the water
questions.explanation: Because interparticle attractions in liquids are slightly weaker than in solids, water particles shift aside and then rejoin.

questions.question: What is the 'boiling point' of a liquid?
options: The temperature at which evaporation stops
The temperature at which a solid melts
The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid boils rapidly and converts into vapour at atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes BOILING from EVAPORATION?
options: Boiling is slow and happens only at the surface; evaporation is fast
There is no difference between boiling and evaporation
Boiling is fast and happens throughout the liquid; evaporation is slow and happens only at the surface
questions.explanation: Boiling is rapid and forms vapour both at the surface and inside the liquid (bubbles), while evaporation is slow and occurs only at the surface at all temperatures.

questions.question: Evaporation of a liquid takes place:
options: At all temperatures, slowly and only from the surface
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens slowly at the surface of a liquid at all temperatures.

questions.question: Why does water spilled on a floor dry up after some time without boiling?
options: Because water turns into a solid
Because floor tiles destroy water particles
Because of evaporation at room temperature
questions.explanation: Spilled water disappears through evaporation, as surface particles slowly escape into the air.

questions.question: What visible sign shows that vapour is forming inside the liquid at its boiling point?
options: Formation of bubbles throughout the liquid
questions.explanation: At the boiling point, rapid vapour formation inside the bulk liquid appears as bubbles rising to the surface.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between solids and liquids (Exercise Q1)?
options: Solids can flow while liquids cannot
Particles are closely packed in solids, while they move past each other in liquids
Particles are far apart in solids and fixed in liquids
Liquids have stronger attractions than solids
questions.explanation: In solids, particles are closely packed in fixed positions, whereas in liquids they can move past each other.

questions.question: When milk in a glass tumbler spills on a table, the milk spreads out while the glass tumbler keeps its shape. Why?
options: Glass has weaker attractions than milk
Milk is a liquid whose particles slide past each other, while glass is a solid with fixed particles
Milk is a gas at room temperature
questions.explanation: Milk is a liquid (fluid) that flows easily, while the glass tumbler is a rigid solid.

questions.question: Why does water take the shape of your folded hands when held, but flow away when you open your hands?
options: Water has no fixed shape and its particles are free to flow
questions.explanation: Water is a liquid, so it takes the shape of whatever holds it and flows away once released.

questions.question: How strong are the interparticle attractions in liquids compared to solids and gases?
options: Slightly weaker than in solids, but much stronger than in gases
questions.explanation: Interparticle attractions are strongest in solids, slightly weaker in liquids, and negligible in gases.

questions.question: Which substance from Exercise Q7 is a LIQUID at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Glycerin is a liquid whose particles are slightly loosely packed and move within a limited space.

questions.question: Why do liquids keep a definite volume even though they have no fixed shape?
options: They turn into solids inside a bottle
Their particles cannot move at all
Air pushes them down from above
Interparticle attractions are still strong enough to keep particles within a limited space
questions.explanation: Liquid particles can slide past each other (no fixed shape), yet attractions keep them close together (definite volume).

questions.question: What happens to liquid particles when heated to the boiling point?
options: They move so vigorously that attractions weaken and particles escape as vapour
questions.explanation: At the boiling point, vigorous particle movement overcomes interparticle attractions and particles escape as gas/vapour.

questions.question: Which state of wax is seen right near the wick of a burning candle?
questions.explanation: A burning candle shows solid wax in the body, molten liquid wax near the wick, and wax vapour around the flame.

questions.question: Compared to solids, the interparticle spacing in liquids is:
options: Ten times smaller than in solids
A little more than in solids (except water vs. ice)
questions.explanation: Liquid particles are slightly loosely packed with a little more spacing than solids (with ice being an exception).

questions.question: Why are liquids like water practically incompressible inside a sealed syringe?
options: Liquid particles are already close together with very little free space between them
Water turns into iron under pressure
questions.explanation: Unlike gases, liquid particles have very little empty space between them, so pressing the plunger barely changes their volume.

questions.question: What are the shape and volume of a gas?
options: Neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume
questions.explanation: Gases take the shape of their container and expand to fill all available space, so they have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.

questions.question: In Activity 7.5, when the glass plate between Gas Jar A (filled with incense smoke) and Gas Jar B (empty) is removed, what happens?
options: The smoke stays only inside Gas Jar A
The smoke turns into liquid water
The smoke spreads freely to fill all of Gas Jar B as well
questions.explanation: The smoke spreads into Gas Jar B and fills the entire space, showing gases have no fixed volume and move freely.

questions.question: In Activity 7.5, how does smoke help us see the movement of invisible gas particles?
options: Tiny visible smoke particles in air are constantly hit by invisible gas particles
questions.explanation: Tiny smoke particles suspended in air are constantly struck by invisible moving gas particles, showing us how gases move.

questions.question: Which coloured vapour is mentioned in NCERT Curiosity as an alternative to incense smoke in a closed gas jar (Fig. 7.8)?
questions.explanation: Placing some solid iodine in a closed gas jar produces visible iodine vapour that spreads throughout the jar.

questions.question: What safety precaution is given in NCERT Curiosity while using solid iodine?
options: Be careful because iodine vapours can cause irritation
questions.explanation: The Safety First box warns to be careful with solid iodine because its vapours can cause irritation.

questions.question: Why are BOTH liquids and gases classified together as 'fluids'?
options: Both can flow and do not retain a fixed shape
questions.explanation: Both liquids and gases flow and do not keep a fixed shape, which sets them apart from solids and classifies them as fluids.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fluid?
questions.explanation: Rock salt is a solid with a fixed shape; liquids (water, glycerin) and gases (air) are fluids.

questions.question: How strong are the interparticle attractions in gases?
questions.explanation: In gases, particles are very far apart and interparticle attractions are negligible (minimum).

questions.question: In Activity 7.6 (syringe without a needle), pushing the plunger while closing the open end with your thumb shows that:
options: Air volume decreases because gas particles have large spaces between them
questions.explanation: Pushing the plunger forces gas particles closer together, proving gases have large interparticle spaces and are compressible.

questions.question: In Activity 7.6, what happens when you stop pushing the syringe plunger filled with compressed air?
options: Gas particles spread out again and push the plunger back to its original position
questions.explanation: When external pressure is removed, moving gas particles spread back out and push the plunger to its original position.

questions.question: What happens when you repeat Activity 7.6 by filling the syringe with WATER instead of air?
options: Water compresses more easily than air
questions.explanation: Testing the syringe with water shows that liquids are practically incompressible compared to gases.

questions.question: In which state of matter is the interparticle spacing MAXIMUM?
questions.explanation: Gases have the maximum interparticle spacing and complete freedom of particle movement.

questions.question: Arrange Solid, Liquid, and Gas in DECREASING order of compressibility:
questions.explanation: Gases are highly compressible, liquids are practically incompressible, and solids are rigid and virtually incompressible.

questions.question: Why do gases mix with each other very easily, whereas solids do not?
options: Gases have stronger attractions than solids
Gas particles are heavier than solid particles
Gas particles have large spaces, negligible attraction, and move freely in all directions
questions.explanation: Free movement in all directions and huge interparticle spaces allow gas particles to mix rapidly.

questions.question: Which substance from Exercise Q7 is a GAS at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Methane is a gas at room temperature with maximum interparticle spacing and negligible attraction.

questions.question: Why can a large amount of cooking gas (LPG) or oxygen be packed into a small cylinder?
options: Gases have large interparticle spaces and can be compressed under pressure
Gases turn into iron inside cylinders
questions.explanation: High compressibility due to large interparticle spaces allows large volumes of gas to be stored in cylinders under pressure.

questions.question: If 100 mL of a gas is transferred into an empty 1-litre flask, what will be the volume of the gas now?
questions.explanation: Gases have no fixed volume—they always expand to occupy the entire available space of their container.

questions.question: How do gas particles move inside a closed container?
options: They settle at the bottom like sand
They move freely in all directions, filling the entire container
They stick only to the lid
questions.explanation: Gas particles have enough thermal energy to overcome attractions and move freely in all directions.

questions.question: Why do gas particles have complete freedom of movement?
options: Their thermal energy is high enough to overcome interparticle attractions
Gravity does not act on gases
questions.explanation: High thermal energy lets gas particles overcome interparticle attractive forces and move freely everywhere.

questions.question: When a burning candle is blown out, the white wispy smoke rising from the wick is mainly:
options: Wax vapour (gaseous state of wax) mixing with air
questions.explanation: A candle shows all three states of wax: solid wax, molten liquid wax, and rising wax vapour (gas).

questions.question: Which everyday object shows all three states of the SAME substance (solid, liquid, and gas) at once?
options: A burning candle (solid wax, molten wax, wax vapour)
questions.explanation: Exercise Q8 highlights a burning candle as an example showing solid wax, molten liquid wax, and gaseous wax vapour together.

questions.question: What are the tiny empty gaps present between the constituent particles of matter called?
questions.explanation: The spaces present between constituent particles of matter are called interparticle spaces.

questions.question: What is present inside the interparticle spaces between the particles of a solid?
questions.explanation: NCERT Curiosity clearly states that interparticle spaces contain NOTHING at all—they are not filled with air.

questions.question: In Activity 7.7, water is marked at level A, sugar is added raising it to B, and after stirring to dissolve the sugar, level C is marked. How does level C compare to level B?
options: Level C drops slightly below B
Level C rises much higher than B
questions.explanation: After dissolving, sugar particles occupy the interparticle spaces between water particles, so level C drops slightly below B.

questions.question: In Activity 7.7, why is the final volume of sugar solution LESS than the sum of the volumes of water and sugar?
options: Dissolved sugar particles fit into the interparticle spaces between water particles
questions.explanation: Because sugar particles occupy the available interparticle spaces between water particles, the total volume is less than the separate sum.

questions.question: In Activity 7.7, which tool is used to stir the sugar in the glass vessel?
questions.explanation: A glass rod is used to stir and dissolve the sugar in Activity 7.7 (Fig. 7.10c).

questions.question: Which group contains ONLY soluble solids mentioned in Activity 7.7?
questions.explanation: Activity 7.7 names sugar, common salt, and glucose as soluble solids, and sand and stone pieces as insoluble solids.

questions.question: What happens to the water level when insoluble SAND is added and stirred in a beaker of water?
options: The water level drops to zero
Sand settles at the bottom and increases the total water level
Sand dissolves and lowers the level
questions.explanation: Because sand does not dissolve, its grains settle at the bottom and take up space, increasing the total level.

questions.question: Both sugar and sand are solids. Why does sugar dissolve in water while sand does NOT?
options: Water particles stop moving around sand
In sand, constituent particles are held together so strongly that water particles cannot pull them out
Sand is not made of particles
questions.explanation: In insoluble solids like sand, constituent particles are bound too strongly for moving water particles to pull them apart.

questions.question: Which of the following solids will settle at the bottom and raise the water level without dissolving?
questions.explanation: Stone pieces are insoluble in water, so they settle at the bottom and displace water upward.

questions.question: Do closely packed solids still have any interparticle space between their particles?
options: Yes, small empty interparticle spaces remain even in closely packed solids
questions.explanation: Fig. 7.12a shows that even closely packed solids have tiny empty interparticle spaces between their particles.

questions.question: Arrange Solid, Liquid, and Gas in INCREASING order of interparticle spaces:
questions.explanation: Interparticle space is minimum in solids, slightly more in liquids, and maximum in gases.

questions.question: Arrange Solid, Liquid, and Gas in DECREASING order of interparticle spaces:
questions.explanation: Gases have the largest interparticle spaces, followed by liquids, and solids have the smallest spaces.

questions.question: In 'A Step Further' (air pollution studies), what is the full form of SPM?
questions.explanation: SPM stands for Suspended Particulate Matter—tiny dust particles suspended in the air.

questions.question: Is a tiny dust particle of SPM the same as a constituent particle (atom or molecule) of matter?
options: No, even one tiny SPM dust particle is made of a very large number of atoms and molecules
Yes, one dust particle is a single atom
No, SPM is a pure liquid
questions.explanation: SPM dust particles are far larger than constituent particles—each dust speck contains a huge number of atoms and molecules.

questions.question: What are the ultra-tiny constituent particles that make up even a single dust speck of SPM?
questions.explanation: Even a tiny dust particle is made of a very large number of constituent particles—atoms and molecules.

questions.question: In Fig. 7.11, how are dissolved sugar particles shown inside water?
options: Evenly distributed in the interparticle spaces between water particles
questions.explanation: Fig. 7.11 shows tiny sugar particles nestled evenly inside the spaces between water particles.

questions.question: If you add two spoons of glucose to water and stir well, what happens to the water level after dissolving?
options: It drops slightly compared to the level right after adding undissolved glucose
questions.explanation: Just like sugar and salt, glucose dissolves and its particles occupy the interparticle spaces of water.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE according to NCERT Chapter 7?
options: Interparticle spaces in solids are filled with air
Sugar particles occupy interparticle spaces in water
Gases have the largest interparticle spaces
Interparticle spaces are smallest in solids
questions.explanation: Interparticle spaces contain nothing at all—it is a misconception to think they are filled with air.

questions.question: When common salt dissolves completely in water, why does the water level NOT rise by the full volume of the salt?
options: Salt particles fit into the interparticle spaces between water particles
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt particles occupy existing interparticle spaces among water particles.

questions.question: Why does increasing the interparticle space turn a solid into a liquid or a gas?
options: Interparticle attractive forces weaken drastically as distance increases
questions.explanation: Greater spacing drastically weakens interparticle attractions, allowing particles to move more freely.

questions.question: Which activity directly proves that there are empty interparticle spaces between water particles?
options: Activity 7.7 (marking water levels A, B, and C with sugar)
questions.explanation: Activity 7.7 tracks water levels A, B, and C before and after dissolving sugar to show interparticle spaces in water.

questions.question: Why is the volume increase permanent when sand is stirred into water, unlike sugar?
options: Sand particles cannot break apart to enter water's interparticle spaces
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble, so its grains stay intact at the bottom and displace water, keeping the level raised.

questions.question: In Fig. 7.12, which state of matter shows particles very far apart with huge empty spaces between them?
questions.explanation: Fig. 7.12c represents the gaseous state, where interparticle spaces are maximum.

questions.question: Which statement correctly links interparticle spacing and interparticle attraction?
options: Smaller spacing → Stronger attraction (Solids); Larger spacing → Weaker attraction (Gases)
Spacing has no effect on attraction
questions.explanation: Closely packed particles (solids) have the strongest attractions, while far-apart particles (gases) have negligible attractions.

questions.question: In Activity 7.8, what colour spreads through still water when a few grains of potassium permanganate are dropped in?
questions.explanation: Streaks of pink colour spread out from the grain until the entire water turns a uniform pink colour.

questions.question: Why does potassium permanganate spread throughout still water even without stirring (Activity 7.8)?
options: Constantly moving water particles pull out potassium permanganate particles and hit them until they spread evenly
questions.explanation: Water particles are always in motion—they pull out potassium permanganate particles from the grain and collide with them to spread them evenly.

questions.question: What safety precaution must be followed while handling potassium permanganate in Activity 7.8?
options: Heat it directly on a palm
Do not touch it with bare hands; use a spoon or spatula
questions.explanation: The Safety First box warns not to touch potassium permanganate with bare hands and to use a spoon or spatula.

questions.question: In 'Think Like a Scientist', potassium permanganate is added to hot water, room-temperature water, and ice-cold water. Where does it spread the FASTEST?
questions.explanation: Water particles move fastest in hot water and slowest in ice-cold water, so the pink colour spreads fastest in hot water.

questions.question: Where does potassium permanganate spread the SLOWEST among hot water, room-temperature water, and ice-cold water?
options: It does not spread in any water
questions.explanation: In ice-cold water, particles have the least thermal energy and move the slowest.

questions.question: What does the hot-vs-cold water potassium permanganate experiment prove?
options: Cold water has more heat energy than hot water
Temperature has no effect on particles
Providing heat (thermal energy) increases the speed of particle movement
questions.explanation: Supplying heat increases thermal energy, making constituent particles move faster.

questions.question: In Activity 7.9, why does the fragrance of an incense stick lit in one corner reach the entire room?
options: Constantly moving air particles hit the fragrance particles and carry them throughout the room
questions.explanation: Air particles are always moving; they collide with fragrance particles and spread them across the whole room.

questions.question: How do soap particles remove oil stains from clothes ('Ever Heard Of...', Fig. 7.15)?
options: Soap particles surround the oil—one end attaches to oil and the other mixes with water to wash it away
Soap turns oil into solid sand
Soap only changes the colour of oil
questions.explanation: Each soap particle has one end that attaches to oil and another end that mixes with water, lifting and rinsing oil stains away.

questions.question: Why can plain water alone NOT wash away an oil stain easily without soap?
options: Oil dissolves instantly in cold water
Water particles cannot attach to oil; soap particles bridge oil and water
questions.explanation: Oil does not mix with plain water, whereas soap particles attach to both oil and water to lift the stain off.

questions.question: Exercise Q2 states: 'On heating camphor, energy is released as a smell.' Is this statement TRUE or FALSE?
options: False — heating gives camphor particles thermal energy so they escape as vapour particles that reach our nose
True — energy itself turns into smell
questions.explanation: Smell is not energy being released; heating converts camphor into vapour particles that travel through the air to our nose.

questions.question: When camphor is heated in one corner of a room, why does its smell reach every corner?
options: Camphor vapour particles move freely and spread throughout the air
Solid camphor jumps across the room
questions.explanation: Heating turns camphor into vapour whose particles move freely and spread across the entire room.

questions.question: According to Page 112 of NCERT Curiosity, what single factor governs interparticle spacing, attraction strength, and the state of matter?
questions.explanation: Thermal energy controls particle motion and spacing, which in turn determines attraction strength and physical state.

questions.question: Why does the smell of hot food reach you from a distance much faster than cold food?
options: Particles from hot food have more thermal energy and move faster through air
Cold food is heavier than iron
questions.explanation: Higher temperature gives aroma particles more thermal energy, so they move and spread much faster.

questions.question: In which state of matter is particle movement described as 'negligible (only vibrations)'?
questions.explanation: The summary on Page 112 states that particle movement in solids is negligible (only vibrations in fixed positions).

questions.question: In which state of matter is particle movement 'restricted to a limited space'?
questions.explanation: In liquids, particles move past each other freely but stay within a limited space.

questions.question: In which state of matter can particles move freely in 'all the available space'?
questions.explanation: Gas particles have negligible attraction and move freely in all available space.

questions.question: Why does perfume sprayed in one corner of a classroom quickly reach students sitting far away?
options: Perfume vapour particles mix and collide with constantly moving air particles
Perfume droplets roll along the floor
questions.explanation: Like incense fragrance, perfume vapour particles spread across the room by colliding with constantly moving air particles.

questions.question: If you drop a crystal of potassium permanganate into ice-cold water (2 °C) and another into hot water (70 °C), which turns uniformly pink faster?
options: Both turn pink at the exact same second
Potassium permanganate does not dissolve in hot water
The 70 °C water turns pink much faster because water particles move faster at higher temperatures
questions.explanation: Higher thermal energy in 70 °C water makes particles move faster, spreading the colour much more quickly.

questions.question: When ice melts into water and then boils into steam, what happens to thermal energy and interparticle spacing?
options: Both thermal energy and spacing decrease
Thermal energy increases, weakening attractions so particles move much farther apart
Particles merge into one giant particle
questions.explanation: Heating raises thermal energy from solid to liquid to gas, overcoming attractions and greatly increasing particle spacing.

questions.question: Which option correctly matches a state of matter with its particle properties?
options: Solid → Free motion in all directions
Gas → Negligible attraction, maximum spacing, free motion in all directions
Liquid → Maximum spacing, no fixed volume
questions.explanation: Gases have negligible interparticle attraction, maximum interparticle spacing, and free motion in all directions.

questions.question: Arrange Solid, Liquid, and Gas in INCREASING order of thermal (heat) energy of particles for the same substance (ice, water, steam):
questions.explanation: Thermal energy is lowest in solids, higher in liquids, and highest in gases.
